title: What We Learned Deploying AI within Bloomberg’s Engineering Organization – Lei Zhang, Bloomberg

summary:
Lei Zhang leads Bloomberg's Technology Infrastructure department, covering data centers, connectivity, developer productivity, and reliability solutions. Bloomberg operates at massive scale with 9,000+ software engineers, handles 600 billion market messages, employs 500+ people focused on AI products, maintains one of the world's largest private networks and JavaScript codebases, and contributes to open source including the Envoy AI gateway.

Bloomberg began AI for coding exploration over two years ago amid an overwhelming landscape of tools. Initial productivity surveys showed quick gains in proof-of-concept work, tests, and one-time scripts, but gains dropped sharply beyond greenfield scenarios. With codebases of hundreds of millions of lines, system complexity grows exponentially, requiring careful approaches.

Bloomberg identified higher-ROI areas beyond raw code generation. Uplift agents scan codebases to apply patches with reasoning, improving on regex-based refactoring. Challenges include lack of deterministic verification, increased open PRs and merge times, and a shift from 'how' to 'what' thinking. Incident response agents leverage LLMs' speed and unbiased analysis across codebases, telemetry, feature flags, and call traces.

To prevent duplication—e.g., 10 teams building PR review bots—Bloomberg partnered with its AI organization to create a 'paved path': an AI gateway for model experimentation and selection, an MCP discovery hub to avoid duplicate tool building, and a standardized platform service for MCP server creation and deployment with authentication and security. The platform separates easy POCs from production, which requires quality control.

Bloomberg drove adoption through multiple levers. Its 20+ year training program incorporated AI coding into onboarding, making new hires change agents who challenge senior engineers. Champ and guild programs—cross-organization tech communities running 10+ years—were leveraged to bootstrap an engineer AI productivity community two years back, enabling shared learning and organic effort duplication. Inner source contributions and a 'visit engineer' program, where engineers rotate to another team for six months to a year, help address prioritization mismatches.

Data revealed that individual contributors show stronger AI adoption than leadership teams. Many software TLS and managers lack sufficient AI experience to guide their teams effectively, prompting Bloomberg to roll out leadership workshops. Zhang closes by noting that AI changes the cost function of software engineering—some work becomes cheaper, some more expensive—creating an opportunity to revisit basic principles and ask what high-quality software engineering truly means.

sections.title: Introduction to Bloomberg's Scale & Infrastructure
sections.summary: Lei Zhang introduces Bloomberg's scale: 9,000+ engineers, 600 billion market messages, 500+ AI-focused employees, one of the largest private networks and JavaScript codebases, and open source contributions including Envoy AI gateway.

sections.title: AI for Coding: Initial Adoption & The Greenfield Drop-off
sections.summary: Bloomberg started AI for coding ~2 years ago amid overwhelming tooling options. Initial surveys showed gains in POCs, tests, and one-time scripts, but productivity measurements dropped quickly beyond greenfield work. System complexity with hundreds of millions of lines of code demands careful approaches.

sections.title: Uplift Agents: Automating Refactoring & Maintenance
sections.summary: Uplift agents scan codebases to apply patches with reasoning, improving on regex-based refactoring. Challenges include lack of deterministic verification, increased open PRs and merge times, and a shift from 'how' to 'what' thinking in engineering.

sections.title: Incident Response Agents: Unbiased Troubleshooting & Speed
sections.summary: Incident response agents leverage LLMs' speed and unbiased analysis to quickly traverse codebases, telemetry, feature flags, and call traces. Multiple teams wanting to build similar agents creates duplication risk, motivating a coordinated platform approach.

sections.title: The 'Paved Path': Standardizing AI Tool Building
sections.summary: Bloomberg created a paved path with an AI gateway for model selection, an MCP discovery hub to prevent duplicate tool building, and a standardized deployment platform. Philosophy: make the right thing easy, the wrong thing hard. Easy POCs are separated from production quality control.

sections.title: Leveraging Training & Communities for Adoption
sections.summary: Bloomberg leveraged its 20+ year training program by incorporating AI coding into onboarding, showing engineers how to best use AI tools with Bloomberg's principles and technologies to drive adoption.

sections.title: Community Programs, Leadership Gap & The Changing Cost Function
sections.summary: Training makes new hires change agents who challenge senior engineers. Champ and guild programs (10+ years) bootstrapped an AI productivity community 2 years ago for shared learning and organic effort duplication. Inner source and 'visit engineer' rotations address prioritization mismatches. Data shows individual contributors adopt AI faster than leadership, prompting leadership workshops. Zhang closes noting AI changes the cost function of software engineering, creating an opportunity to revisit basic principles of high-quality engineering.
